title: Bare promises
author: Tom Stafford
summary: Stafford walks through two Charness and Dufwenberg experiments to make a claim about why communication persuades, and it is not the information it carries. In the original trust game, letting the second player send a single free-form message roughly doubles the rate at which the pair actually cooperates, and messages containing a promise push the first player's willingness to commit to ninety-two percent, despite the promise binding nobody to anything. The follow-up study is the twist the essay is built around: when the researchers replaced the free message with a pre-printed slip reading I promise to choose Roll, the effect vanished entirely. Same semantic content, same implied commitment, no result. Stafford reads this through costly signalling, concluding that a signal only carries weight when the sender spent something to send it, even something as trivial as writing the words out by hand. He closes by pointing the finding at a live question, which is what happens to trust when you hand the writing of your messages to a machine that can produce a longer and more polished version at no cost to you.
points: Sets up the puzzle with the standard finding that people cooperate in one-shot trust games far more than economic rationality predicts.
Shows a single unbinding message more than doubles successful cooperation, and a message containing a promise drives the partner's commitment rate to ninety-two percent.
Uses the pre-printed bare promise condition as the decisive contrast, since identical wording with no effort behind it moves nothing.
Extracts the general rule that signals must cost the sender something to carry meaning, which is why the gesture and not the words does the work.
Turns the result on outsourced writing, warning that a more impressive message someone or something else produced may buy less trust than it appears to.
quotes: The second thing about this kind of trust game is that consistently, all around the world, in different cultures and populations, people cooperate more than economic rationality says they should.
The ability to send just one message produces big shifts in A’s behaviour, and that in turn produces big shifts in the overall levels of cooperation
They found for messages where B makes a promise A’s IN rate is a massive 92% (and the eventual cooperate rate is 67%).
This bare promise condition shows that promises, like all communication, are not just the semantic content.
For participants it matters not just what is said in the promise, but that the person promising has made an effort, even as minimal an effort as to write out “I promise”.
There’s a principle here. For signals to matter, they should cost something to the sender
to write a longer, more professional, more impressive, message, but when you want people to trust what you are saying, this might be less of the shortcut than it appears.
